summary:
Romania is broadly workable for a transgender visitor, with same-sex relations legal nationwide and a protection apparatus that functions unevenly. Domestic legal gender recognition exists and is court-based, but civil-status authorities resist it in practice. In the Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi case, the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate reflecting the trans man's UK-recognised identity, and the Bucharest Tribunal rejected the appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates, making the decision definitive in March 2026. ACCEPT Romania announced the outcome on Trans Day of Visibility and urges others who have changed their documents in another European Union member state to pursue transcription in Romania.

The legal anchor is the Court of Justice of the European Union's ruling of October 2024, reported by Reuters, that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights in refusing recognition of a UK gender recognition certificate. ACCEPT Romania describes the underlying obligation as a duty on member states to transcribe legal gender recognition obtained in another EU member state. Whether the same duty extends to recognition obtained outside the Union is not established by the sources reviewed.

One definitive ruling does not amount to uniform practice. The Mirzarafie-Ahi order shows that a Romanian court will issue a corrected birth certificate where a foreign certificate is recognised, and it also shows that regional civil-status directorates were prepared to appeal rather than comply.

The country's anti-discrimination statute, Government Ordinance 137/2000, covers sex and sexual orientation but does not name gender identity. Enforcement runs through the National Council for Combating Discrimination (CNCD), which has investigated printing houses that refused to produce LGBT and gender-equality materials. Outright International records institutional follow-through on LGBTI complaints as limited.

There is no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions in Romania. The 2018 referendum proposing a constitutional definition of marriage as between a man and a woman failed on low turnout, and the Romanian Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017.

Official rhetoric toward transgender people grew harsher during the 2025 electoral period. Presidential candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself against LGBTQ people in February, Prime Minister Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes, and a deputy mayor from the AUR party in Ploiești made further derogatory announcements. The National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August 2025 after ACCEPT complained about anti-Pride framing presented as provocation. ILGA-Europe and partners reported that eight of nine country submissions to the European Union's 2025 Rule of Law Report documented smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people, with the Romanian election period cited as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.

Visible hostility coexists with visible organising. Tens of thousands marched at Bucharest Pride in June 2025 as it marked its twentieth anniversary, at a point organisers described as growing right-wing hostility toward LGBTQ+ Romanians.
tangentialFactors:
The Council of Europe published a thematic review in January 2023 titled 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania', a national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 that covers legal and policy frameworks alongside applicable European Court of Human Rights case-law. The report confirms that a monitoring and implementation process exists at state level, but the sources reviewed do not record outcomes of any trans-specific prosecution under it.

A FRA-commissioned legal study from February 2008, authored by Romanița Elena Iordache and Iustina Ionescu, maps how Romanian law implemented the EU Employment Directive 2000/78/EC and free-movement rules for LGBT partners, including national anti-discrimination concepts, CNCD enforcement powers and NGO complaint routes. It remains a dated baseline for the protection architecture rather than a statement of current law.

Public opinion is more supportive than the political class suggests. An IPSOS PRIDE survey from 2023 found that 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition, while LGBTI organisations continue to register and operate.

Contestation over equality provisions extends beyond LGBTI policy. Draft education-law amendments carrying anti-discrimination provisions in March 2024 drew protests from thirteen religious groups and drew a counter-response from an organisation of people over fifty.

The surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period is presented in the EU Rule of Law reporting as one instance of a pattern, since eight of nine country submissions described smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people.
localsOnly:
Romanian law recognises legal gender recognition, and residents can petition the courts for a corrected birth certificate; the Cluj civil-status directorates' attempt to block the Mirzarafie-Ahi order shows that administrative resistance remains a live obstacle for residents as well as visitors.

Government Ordinance 137/2000 provides anti-discrimination protection on the grounds of sex and sexual orientation, and complaints are handled by the CNCD, which holds investigatory powers and has used them against businesses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials. Gender identity is not named as a protected ground in the ordinance.

Employment discrimination and free-movement rules affecting LGBT partners sit under the framework mapped in the 2008 FRA-commissioned study, which documented CNCD enforcement powers and NGO complaint mechanisms.

Same-sex couples have no access to marriage or civil partnership. A civil-partnership bill has been blocked by the Romanian Orthodox Church's opposition since 2017, and the 2018 referendum on a constitutional marriage definition failed because of low turnout.

LGBTI organisations can register and operate in Romania, and ACCEPT Romania remains active in litigation, regulatory complaints and public advocacy, including the complaint that produced the National Audiovisual Council's warning to B1 TV.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Romanian courts will transcribe gender recognition obtained outside the European Union, including from the United Kingdom, is unresolved by the sources reviewed. The CJEU ruling and the Romanian court order both turn on recognition obtained within or attached to the Union's framework, and no source here addresses non-EU certificates.

No source reviewed states whether Government Ordinance 137/2000 will be amended to name gender identity as a protected ground, or whether the civil-partnership bill will advance. Both are presented as current obstacles, not as pending developments with dates.

Whether the hate-crime legal framework has been applied to offences against transgender people is not established by this inventory. The Council of Europe thematic review documents a framework and implementation reporting, and the sources record no prosecution outcomes.

Enforcement patterns outside Bucharest and Cluj are not sourced. The evidence of civil-status resistance comes from one directorate pair, and the evidence of protective judicial practice comes from a Bucharest court, so neither can be generalised to the whole country.

Trans-specific violence statistics, health-care access, facility rules and entry or screening requirements for transgender travellers are not covered by the source inventory and cannot be stated here.

The FRA legal study dates from 2008 and the Council of Europe review from a 2023 national self-report; both should be read as dated or self-reported material rather than current independent assessment.
